proofs.title: Rigorous bounds for the larger library sizes
proofs.summary: Numerical source orders are separate from bounds valid for every state in the full partition.
proofs.bodyHtml:
The Schmidt bound gives t\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor. Put s=\lfloor t/2\rfloor. The spin-tensor Gram argument requires (s+1)^2\le n+1, giving the second upper bound above. For odd n\ge5, the complement obstruction strengthens the first bound to (n-3)/2.

The largest-part moment bounds and the full-partition second-order saturation restriction can lower these caps further. First-order existence comes from the finite-filter theorem or the balanced Dicke state. The exact families below improve some lower bounds. A source-reported numerical order is never used as an exact witness in these inequalities.

Bound calculation

proofs.title: Exact families supporting larger-size lower bounds
proofs.summary: Some library partitions admit analytic witnesses independently of the imported numerical data.
proofs.bodyHtml:
For even n\ge8, this state is third-order AC. Symmetry sets the first and third centered moments to zero; its variance is n(n+2)/12. The three Dicke indices are separated by at least four, so all off-diagonal reduced-matrix conditions through order three vanish.

Its Majorana polynomial is a quadratic in z^{n/2}. Both roots are nonzero and distinct: the discriminant is proportional to (n-1)\binom n{n/2}-(n+2)>0. All n Majorana points are therefore simple. This proves t_{\max}(n,(1^n))\ge3.

For n=3g+1, the two-term state on indices g,n, with probabilities n/[2(n-g)] and (n-2g)/[2(n-g)], is second-order AC and has full partition (g,1^{n-g}). The support gap n-g=2g+1\ge3 removes the off-diagonal conditions.

proofs.title: Which full partitions exclude all positive AC orders?
proofs.summary: A point containing at least half the qubits rules out first order, except for the balanced two-point partition.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Rotate a point of multiplicity g so the Dicke distribution has support K\ge g. First-order anticoherence requires \mathbb E[K]=n/2. This is impossible if g>n/2. If g=n/2, every nonzero amplitude must have K=n/2, so the state is a rotated balanced Dicke state, with exactly two distinct points of multiplicity n/2.

All other partitions at the half-size boundary are therefore excluded, even though their largest multiplicity meets the coarse bound. Conversely, the balanced Dicke state is first-order anticoherent. A value zero means no positive AC order; the partition itself is a valid symmetric-state partition.

references.location: Majorana-degeneracy exclusion criterion. The finite-filter existence argument is independently supplied here.

proofs.title: Every partition strictly below the half-size boundary admits first order
proofs.summary: A finite invertible collective filter produces a first-order AC representative while preserving every multiplicity.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Start with any normalized symmetric state having the desired full partition. Minimize \|A^{\otimes n}\psi\|^2 over A\in\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb C). Write A=U\operatorname{diag}(e^{s/2},e^{-s/2})V, with s\ge0 and U,V\in\mathrm{SU}(2). The left unitary does not affect the norm.

For every V, the rotated state has a strictly positive total probability in the positive-J_z subspace. Otherwise all Dicke coefficients with K<n/2 would vanish, producing a pole of multiplicity at least \lceil n/2\rceil, contrary to the hypothesis. This probability is continuous on compact \mathrm{SU}(2), so it has a strictly positive uniform lower bound \epsilon. The filtered norm is at least \epsilon e^{2s m_*}, where m_*>0 is the smallest positive spin eigenvalue, and hence diverges as s\to\infty.

A finite minimizer therefore exists. Varying it on the left along each Hermitian traceless direction gives \langle J_x\rangle=\langle J_y\rangle=\langle J_z\rangle=0 in the normalized filtered state. The filter is invertible, so its action on the projective line preserves distinctness and every point multiplicity. This proves existence within the exact partition, without requiring displayed Dicke coefficients.

The strict inequality matters: at the half-size boundary, a minimizing sequence can change the partition in its limit. That boundary is treated by the separate exclusion argument.

proofs.title: Saturating the second-order bound fixes the full partition
proofs.summary: At n = 3g + 1, only one partition with largest part g can attain second order.
proofs.bodyHtml:
In the pole frame, (K-g)(n-K)\ge0, and second-order anticoherence fixes its expectation to n(n-1-3g)/6. At n=3g+1, this expectation is zero. Hence the support is contained in \{g,n\}. Both endpoint probabilities are nonzero because the mean is n/2.

The Majorana polynomial is therefore z^g(a+bz^{n-g}) with ab\ne0. It has one root of multiplicity g, exactly n-g simple nonzero roots, and no root at infinity. Consequently every other full partition with largest part g has maximal AC order at most one.

This distinguishes, for example, the seven-qubit patterns (2,1^5) and (2^2,1^3): the former attains order two; the latter has maximum one.

proofs.title: How each maximum or rigorous interval is obtained
proofs.summary: Witnesses must match the entire partition. Universal bounds can still use its largest part.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Every integer partition of n is realized by some symmetric pure state, so order zero is always available. The first-order theorems decide exactly whether a positive order is possible. An attached verified state improves the lower bound only for its own complete multiplicity partition.

If a point multiplicity g=\max\lambda exceeds the proved maximum at order t, no state with that partition can be t-AC. Global AC nonexistence proofs give additional upper bounds. Anticoherence at a higher order implies every lower order, so excluding the next order bounds all higher ones. The saturation theorem gives a further restriction that depends on the complete partition.

A single number is a proved maximum; an interval records a proved lower and upper bound. Failure of a particular witness to reach the next order does not exclude other states with the same partition. A partition is not generally a unique state, rotation orbit, or SLOCC class.

proofs.title: Nine improved lower bounds from exact second-order states
proofs.summary: Six previously unresolved partitions now have proven maximum two. Three eleven-qubit partitions improve from 1–3 to 2–3.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Every new witness has Dicke support separated by at least three indices, so all off-diagonal entries of \rho_2 vanish. The two exact moment identities above, together with normalization, give \rho_2=I_3/3.

At eight qubits, probabilities (7,4,16)/27 on indices (0,3,6), with phase i on the middle coefficient, give partition (2,1^6). At ten qubits, positive amplitudes with probabilities (1/6,1/3,1/2) on indices (0,3,8) give (2,1^8). Exact polynomial gcd calculations establish the remaining simple roots. Both partitions have proven maximum two.

The cyclic family P(z)=z^a(z^3-u)^2(z^3-ku), with u=\sqrt{x}>0, adds (2^3,1^3) at n=9, (2^3,1^4) at n=10, (2^3,1^5) and (2^4,1^3) at n=11, and (3,2^3,1^3) at n=12. A specified integer polynomial and rational isolating interval define k; a rational function fixes x. The certificate proves x>0, k\notin\{0,1\}, and zero remainder for both original moment equations. Thus the two cubics are squarefree and coprime; the poles give the remaining multiplicities. The family with cubic power three, P(z)=(z^3-u)^3(z^3-ku), also gives (3^3,1^3) at n=12, with its own isolated algebraic parameter. The nine-, ten- and twelve-qubit cases attain their rigorous upper bound of two.

A further eleven-qubit state uses probabilities (61/126,1/36,41/84) on (2,5,9). Its two double poles and seven simple finite roots give (2^2,1^7). These three eleven-qubit partitions now satisfy 2\le t_{\max}\le3; no third-order exclusion is inferred.

proofs.title: From a repeated point to exact moment bounds
proofs.summary: A repeated Majorana point forces a truncated Dicke distribution in a suitable pole frame.

Rotate a point of multiplicity g to the pole at which c_0=\cdots=c_{g-1}=0. With \Pr(K=k)=|c_k|^2, the diagonal anticoherence equations fix the first t moments to those of the uniform distribution on 0,\ldots,n.

If a polynomial p of degree at most t is nonnegative on every allowed integer g,\ldots,n, but its uniform expectation is negative, that multiplicity is impossible. All displayed upper bounds have exact rational polynomial certificates. Feasible moment distributions alone do not establish anticoherence.

proofs.title: Second order: a sharp one-third bound
proofs.summary: The variance constraint gives a universal bound, attained by exact witnesses wherever second-order states exist in the core.
proofs.bodyHtml:
On the allowed support, (K-g)(n-K)\ge0. Its expectation in a second-order anticoherent state is n(n-1-3g)/6, giving the bound.

For every n\ge7, put g=\lfloor(n-1)/3\rfloor, \delta=n-3g-1, and L=n-g. The positive amplitudes on Dicke support 0,3,L with probabilities p_0=[9(n-2g)-n\delta]/(18L), p_3=n\delta/[18(L-3)], and p_L=n[3(L-3)-\delta]/[6L(L-3)] attain the bound. The support gaps remove every off-diagonal condition through order two. When \delta=0, the middle amplitude vanishes.

The four-qubit tetrahedral and six-qubit octahedral states cover the smaller admissible sizes. The sizes n=2,3,5 admit no second-order state.

proofs.title: Third order: a positive moment matrix
proofs.summary: A two-by-two positive matrix limits how many points can coincide.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Let X=K-n/2, a=n/2-g, and V=n(n+2)/12. Third-order anticoherence gives \mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^3]=0 and \mathbb E[X^2]=V. The nonnegative weight X+a makes the moment matrix \begin{pmatrix}a&V\\V&aV\end{pmatrix} positive semidefinite. Its determinant V(a^2-V) yields the bound.

At eleven qubits the attaining state is certified by a rational fixed-point argument. At twelve qubits an elementary three-term state attains two with partition (2,2,2,2,2,2). Changing its middle phase gives the same maximal multiplicity with partition (2,2,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1).

proofs.title: Schmidt-rank obstruction
proofs.summary: The anticoherent reduction must have full rank in its symmetric subspace; the complementary subsystem must be large enough to accommodate the same Schmidt spectrum.
proofs.bodyHtml: The two complementary reductions have the same nonzero Schmidt spectrum. Anticoherence requires \rho_t=I_{t+1}/(t+1), of rank t+1. The complement is supported on \operatorname{Sym}^{n-t}(\mathbb C^2), of dimension n-t+1. Hence t+1\le n-t+1.

proofs.title: Odd-size complement obstruction
proofs.summary: A one-dimensional complementary kernel would itself have an impossible Schmidt rank.
proofs.bodyHtml:
If \rho_t=I_{t+1}/(t+1), its complement \rho_{t+1} has t+1 equal nonzero eigenvalues in a symmetric space of dimension t+2. Thus \rho_{t+1}=(I_{t+2}-|\phi\rangle\langle\phi|)/(t+1) for a normalized symmetric (t+1)-qubit vector |\phi\rangle.

Trace one qubit, using \operatorname{Tr}_1 I_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(t+1)}=\frac{t+2}{t+1}I_{\mathrm{sym}}^{(t)}. Comparing with \rho_t yields \rho_t^\phi=I_{t+1}/(t+1). But \rho_t^\phi has rank at most two because |\phi\rangle has a single-qubit complement. This contradicts t+1\ge3.

proofs.title: Spin-tensor Gram obstruction
proofs.summary: The spin-tensor Gram matrix gives a quadratic necessary condition on the number of qubits.
proofs.bodyHtml:
Put q=\lfloor t/2\rfloor. For Hilbert–Schmidt orthonormal tensors A,B of ranks at most q, the product A^\dagger B has ranks at most 2q\le t. Anticoherence therefore gives \langle\psi|A^\dagger B|\psi\rangle=\operatorname{Tr}(A^\dagger B)/(n+1).

The (q+1)^2 vectors A|\psi\rangle consequently have a positive diagonal Gram matrix, so they are linearly independent in the (n+1)-dimensional spin space.

proofs.bodyHtml:
For every pure spin-five vector, an exact identity expresses \lVert\psi\rVert^6 as a rational linear combination of twenty cubic scalar contractions of its spin multipoles. Every term contains a multipole of rank 1\le L\le4. Fourth-order anticoherence would make the entire right-hand side zero, contradicting \lVert\psi\rVert^6=1.

Two independent exact calculations establish the identity: one on the symmetric three-copy space, and one by expanding all polynomial coefficients in arbitrary complex amplitudes. No symmetry ansatz or numerical tolerance is used in the final certificate.

proofs.summary: A second exact two-copy identity rules out fifth-order anticoherence.
proofs.bodyHtml: Fifth-order anticoherence sets a_1,\ldots,a_5 to zero, forcing p_6=-27/187. A probability cannot be negative. The coefficient identity is checked with exact rational arithmetic.

proofs.title: Eleven qubits cannot be fourth-order AC
proofs.summary: Two exact three-copy certificates exclude fourth-order anticoherence for arbitrary complex pure symmetric eleven-qubit states.

references.location: Earlier numerical survey; the exact exclusion is independently derived in this catalogue.

proofs.bodyHtml:
A pure fourth-order anticoherent eleven-qubit state would produce a positive, rotation-invariant three-copy operator X with \operatorname{Tr}X=1. Its low-rank multipoles impose twenty-seven necessary equations on twenty-seven real block coordinates. Their integer matrix A satisfies \det A\equiv3\pmod{37}, so it is invertible. The equations force X=0, a contradiction. Taking real parts of positive blocks handles arbitrary complex states.

A second exact certificate expresses \lVert\psi\rVert^6 as a sum of twenty-six cubic multipole invariants. Every term contains a rank between one and four, so fourth-order anticoherence would force 1=0. Its full polynomial expansion is verified coefficientwise with rational arithmetic.

This proves that the maximal order at n=11 is three. Combined with the smaller-size exclusions and a twelve-qubit witness, it also proves that twelve is the first qubit number admitting a pure fourth-order anticoherent state.

Read both proofs and their exact certificates ↗ · LaTeX proof · Polynomial verifier

proofs.title: Four double points at twelve qubits: a restricted exclusion
proofs.summary: Antipodal double-point pairs and rotational symmetry beyond a single half-turn axis are excluded at third order. The general partition remains open.
proofs.bodyHtml:
A rotation puts any two distinct antipodal double-point axes into the stated quartic normal form. For arbitrary complex R, third-order anticoherence forces R to be time-reversal real up to phase: the ten-dimensional odd part of its density matrix maps injectively into the three-qubit reduction. An exact determinant and real-root counts verify this throughout -1<h<1.

The remaining real equations have only the projective solution P=z^2(z^4+1)^2, whose full partition is (2^6), including its double point at infinity. It lies outside the target partition. The proof therefore excludes paired double-point axes, not arbitrary doubled-point geometry.

Separate exact orbit and polynomial arguments also exclude threefold, fourfold and D_2 symmetry. Any hypothetical third-order state in this partition must have proper rotational group C_1 or C_2. Those remaining cases have not been excluded.

The catalogue retains 2\le t_{\max}(12,(2^4,1^4))\le3. An explicit family with the required partition approaches a third-order state in (2^6), so arbitrarily small numerical residuals alone cannot establish attainment.

library.provenanceNote: Imported from Documents/libqiss/ACstates, using the filenames linked in saved copies of the primary pages. The live website timed out; current online byte identity is unverified. Original files are preserved.
library.validationNote: All 144 catalogue vectors were refined at their reported orders, using 100-digit working precision and 85-digit saved coefficients. Independent checks certify the full partitions of the saved vectors; AC remains numerical. Sixteen coordinate/Dicke pairs did not match under the tested conventions: their coordinate-derived representatives appear here, and the original Dicke vectors were refined separately as downloads.
